items.title: GitHub’s model for secret detection: Finding more secrets with less noise
items.author: Batu Ozturkler
items.excerpt: OUR PIPELINE VS. THE PREVIOUS LLM PIPELINESmarter secret scanning, at a fraction of the cost11.5%higher acceptanceOwner-weighted alert precision86%lower median scan execution timePost-push scanning98%lower serving costCompact model vs. remote LLM calls Secret scanning works best when developers are confident in the findings. Catch too little, and real credentials can remain in a repository. Alert too often, and developers may spend time investigating strings that aren’t secrets. Generic secrets make that balance especially difficult. The same string could be a real credential or a documentation placeholder, so detecting it requires understanding the surrounding code and text. To address this challenge, we trained a secret classifier specifically for GitHub’s product needs: distinguishing real credentials from lookalikes while meeting the speed and efficiency requirements of scanning at scale. In our companion post, Secret protection must scale with software, we explained why secret protection must keep pace with AI-accelerated development. Here, we go behind the scenes of the context-aware classifier powering that effort: how we designed, trained, and evaluated it to find more real secrets with less noise. What we enabled GitHub secret scanning operates at two key moments: Push protection helps prevent secrets from entering a repository by scanning changes before a push is accepted, giving developers an opportunity to address the finding. Post-push scanning works after code has been committed, continuously scanning repository content and creating alerts when potential secrets are detected so developers and security teams can investigate and remediate them. We developed a fast classifier that reduced median post-push scan execution time by 86% compared with the previous LLM-based pipeline. That efficiency made it practical to extend generic secret detection to push protection, returning results before developers push changes, not only after code is committed. Secret
items.why_it_matters: GitHub's compact model improves generic secret detection precision at much lower cost. Relevant to repo hygiene on client projects and an instructive case of replacing LLM calls with a small model.

items.title: Anonymous organization-level registries for Dependabot
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now select Anonymous as the authentication method for an organization-level private registry. Use it for registries that Dependabot can reach without credentials, such as an internal package mirror that allows anonymous reads. On github.com, Dependabot update jobs can only reach hosts on the egress allowlist and the private registries you configure. A private registry that’s only defined in a file such as .npmrc or nuget.config is blocked. Organization-level registries apply to every repository you grant access to, including repositories that only use Dependabot security updates and don’t have a dependabot.yml file. To add a registry, go to your organization’s Settings, select Secrets and variables, then Private registries, and choose New private registry. If you used a placeholder token as a workaround, delete that registry and add it again with Anonymous authentication. This is necessary because you can’t change the authentication method of an existing registry. The Anonymous option is now generally available on github.com and will be available in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24. Learn more about giving security features access to private registries and resolving a blocked host in a Dependabot update job. The post Anonymous organization-level registries for Dependabot appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Dependabot now supports anonymous org-level private registries, and registries defined only in .npmrc are blocked. Relevant for client repos using internal npm mirrors and supply-chain hygiene.

items.title: Client telemetry user attribution and configurable capture
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Enterprise administrators can now use telemetry in managed settings to attribute GitHub Copilot activity to a user without collecting their prompts, responses, or tool content. The telemetry.capture.identity setting adds three attributes to OpenTelemetry (OTel) data: user.name: The authenticated Copilot account name, currently the GitHub login. process.user.name: The local operating-system account. host.name: The local machine name. Identity capture is off by default and remains separate from the existing pseudonymous user identifier. Fine-grained capture controls are available in Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and VS Code sessions using Agent Host. Administrators can also independently control five additional capture classes: prompts: User, system, and developer prompts and supported input context. responses: Assistant responses and supported reasoning content. toolArguments: Raw tool arguments, commands, tool schemas, and identifiers for tools, MCP servers, plugins, and hooks. toolOutput: Tool results and execution-error details. policyDetail: Raw policy details such as sandbox filesystem paths. Every capture class is off by default. Explicit managed values take precedence over local settings, SDK configuration, and environment variables. The existing captureContent setting remains available as a legacy shorthand for the five content classes, but it never enables identity. Prompt, tool, and policy capture can include source code, file contents, commands, tool results, and workspace or user-profile paths. Enable only the classes required for your audit use case and send them to an approved collection endpoint. To learn more, see the enterprise managed settings reference and monitor agent usage with OpenTelemetry. Join the discussion within GitHub Community. The post Client telemetry user attribution and configurable capture appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Copilot gained opt-in user identity attribution in OTel telemetry for enterprise admins. This is relevant to clients governing AI coding tool usage and privacy.

items.title: Audit GitHub Code Quality finding dismissals and reopenings
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now review manual dismissals and reopenings of GitHub Code Quality findings in your organization or enterprise audit log. Findings may appear in either your repository’s default-branch backlog or pull requests. Two new events record these actions: repo.code_quality_findings_dismissed records a dismissal of one or more backlog findings. repo.code_quality_findings_reopened records a reopening of one or more backlog findings. Each event includes who made the request, when it happened, the repository and rule, and the identifiers and count of the affected findings. For repositories with Code Quality enabled, you don’t need additional setup. If you have access to your organization audit log or enterprise audit log, filter by these action names to review activity. On GitHub Enterprise Cloud, you can also retrieve these events through the audit log API. This improvement is generally available on GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including enterprises with data residency. It isn’t available on GitHub Enterprise Server. For more on managing findings, see Fixing code quality findings in your repository backlog. Join the GitHub Community discussion. The post Audit GitHub Code Quality finding dismissals and reopenings appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Audit log events for GitHub Code Quality dismissals. Minor governance improvement, useful mainly for enterprise clients with compliance needs.

items.title: Enterprise managed settings enforcement updates
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Enterprise administrators can now require supported GitHub Copilot clients to retrieve current server-managed settings at startup instead of relying on a cached policy. We are also adding minimum client version requirements to governance-focused managed settings keys over time, starting with the sandbox key. Force refresh settings on client startup Set forceRemoteSettingsRefresh to true through server-managed, MDM-managed, or file-based settings when a policy change must take effect before Copilot starts. The setting is supported in Copilot CLI, VS Code, and the GitHub Copilot app. MDM-managed and file-based delivery can require freshness before the client signs in for the first time. A server-managed value begins requiring refreshes on subsequent startups after the client has received it once. While the setting is active, a cached response cannot satisfy the freshness requirement. If the client cannot confirm current policy, it fails closed rather than running with a stale or unconfirmed policy. Without this setting, clients continue to use the normal managed-settings cache for faster startup and resilience during transient service failures. Minimum required client version We’ve also added enforcement of a required minimum client version to the sandbox key in support of the generally available local sandbox capability. When this key is included in managed settings, users who pin to older versions of Copilot clients will now be forced to update in order to resume using Copilot. To learn more, see Deploying enterprise managed settings. Join the discussion within GitHub Community. The post Enterprise managed settings enforcement updates appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Copilot enterprise admins can force a fresh managed-settings fetch at startup and set minimum client versions. Relevant to fractional CTOs advising clients on governing AI coding agents.

items.title: Improved detection for withdrawn Dependabot alerts
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now more easily detect withdrawn Dependabot alerts. Dependabot withdraws and removes an alert when the advisory or vulnerability that produced it is no longer valid. Two changes help you detect these withdrawals: Webhooks: The dependabot_alert webhook event now includes a withdrawn action. The payload contains identifiers captured before the alert was removed, such as the alert number, GHSA and CVE IDs, package, and manifest path. If you already subscribe to dependabot_alert events, you’ll automatically receive these deliveries. REST API: Requests to get or update a withdrawn alert now return 410 Gone instead of 404 Not Found, so you can tell a withdrawn alert apart from one that never existed. These changes are available for all repositories on github.com and will be included in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24. Learn more about the dependabot_alert webhook event and the REST API endpoints for Dependabot alerts. The post Improved detection for withdrawn Dependabot alerts appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Dependabot now emits webhook events and API signals for withdrawn alerts. This helps keep supply-chain alert pipelines and dashboards accurate for client repos on GitHub.

items.author: Allison

New secret scanning partner Salesforce is now a secret scanning partner. When a provider’s secret is found in a public repository, GitHub forwards it to the relevant partner so they can revoke or rotate the credential before it can be abused. Provider Secret type Salesforce salesforce_marketing_cloud_api_oauth2_token Detectors added Secret scanning now automatically detects the following new secret types in your repositories. Provider Secret type Anthropic anthropic_service_api_key Anthropic anthropic_user_api_key Cloudsmith cloudsmith_api_key Partner secrets are automatically reported to the secret issuer when found in public repositories through the secret scanning partnership program. User secrets generate secret scanning alerts when found in public or private repositories. Push protection defaults expanded The following detectors are now included in push protection by default. Repositories with secret scanning enabled, including free public repositories, will have commits containing these secrets automatically blocked. Provider Secret type Anthropic anthropic_service_api_key Anthropic anthropic_user_api_key Learn more Learn more about secret scanning and see the full list of supported secrets in our documentation. Let us know what you think in the community discussion. The post Secret scanning blocks Anthropic keys by default, adds Salesforce appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: Quoting Geoffrey Huntley
items.excerpt: If the agent isn't using my diagnostics library, I could introspect and update AGENTS.md, but there's still a delta, and it'll drift. Instead, I write a pre-commit hook that checks the git diff for direct calls to observability modules that bypass my diagnostics module. Boom: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library. All of a sudden it's ten out of ten. — Geoffrey Huntley, nobody should type code by hand anymore. here's what's left. Tags: coding-agents, generative-ai, git, agentic-engineering, ai, geoffrey-huntley, llms
items.why_it_matters: A practical agent workflow tip: enforce conventions with pre-commit hooks that fail the commit and re-prompt the agent, rather than relying on AGENTS.md alone. It maps directly onto our hooks and gated-review practice.

items.title: Dyna-2: General Purpose Physical Agents with Hour-Long Autonomy — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
items.excerpt: Watch along AIE NYC and join us at AIE CODE in SF next month!This episode includes a live demo of the Taku robot that is best enjoyed on YouTube.Last month, Dyna made waves by announcing Dyna-2, a world-action model pre-trained on one million hours of human video, claiming several new scaling laws on human data across four orders of magnitude. They have now followed up the model with a physical robot agent, Dyna-2.1, that has to be seen to be believed:In his talk at AIE this year, Jason talked about how the real challenge for robotics in the real world is reliable, long-horizon autonomy, and how Dyna got its models to a 99.4% success rate folding restaurant napkins for 24 hours straight, including recovering after it pulled over the whole stack.From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung, Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers.We go deep on Dyna-2, Dyna’s million-hour world-action model that combines future video prediction with robot actions, the scaling laws behind human-to-robot transfer, diffusion transformers and flow matching, and why synthetic environments and self-generated training data could unlock the next wave of robotics progress. Jason also explains why Dyna builds its own hardware instead of relying on off-the-shelf humanoids, how agentic harnesses enable robots to execute hour-long workflows, why dexterous hands and missing sensory data remain major bottlenecks, and what separates real commercial deployments from the graveyard of robotics startups.
